entities.summary: Andrés Laguna de Segovia (1499–1559) was a Spanish humanist physician, pharmacologist, and botanist who made significant contributions to the field of medicine, particularly in the areas of pharmacology and botany. His work on the properties of plants and the use of herbs in medicine was widely recognized and influential during his lifetime. Laguna's findings were also used by later scientists, such as Andreas Vesalius, who built upon his work in his own studies on human anatomy. Laguna's legacy extends beyond his scientific contributions, as he was also a prominent figure in the Spanish court, serving as a physician and advisor to King Philip II. His work and influence had a lasting impact on the development of modern medicine and the understanding of the natural world. Laguna's discovery of the medicinal properties of the American ginseng, for example, was a major breakthrough in the field of pharmacology and paved the way for further research into the uses of native plants. Despite his significant contributions to the field of medicine, Laguna's life was cut short when he died in 1559 at the age of 60. His legacy continues to be celebrated and studied by scholars and scientists today.

entities.summary:
Andrés Laguna de Segovia (1499–1559) was a Spanish humanist physician, pharmacologist, and classicist who translated and commented on Dioscorides and served in European courts, including papal and Habsburg circles. His medical humanism joined philological recovery of ancient pharmacy to clinical and botanical observation in the Renaissance.

Laguna’s annotated Dioscorides became a major Iberian vehicle for learned pharmacology, circulating knowledge of simples amid New World botanical encounters. As a converso-era Spanish intellectual abroad, he also navigates the mobility of physicians in mid-sixteenth-century Catholic Europe.

He stands among Spain’s foremost Renaissance medical humanists—linking Segovia to the wider republic of medical letters.
